title: Jitter-aware admission limiter and attention micro-slicing to reduce tail latency in continuous batching
creator: Aisha Kapoor
description:
Problem:
Current continuous-batching admission logic sometimes accepts small bursts that interleave with long-running batches, causing large jitter spikes in the tail (p95–p999). These spikes are most visible on heterogeneous workloads (short chat messages mixed with long-streaming generations) where attention compute and kernel selection change dramatically between requests.

Goals:
- Reduce p95/p99 tail latency by smoothing admission jitter without degrading median latency.
- Preserve throughput and GPU utilization for heavy decodes.
- Integrate with kernel selection so we avoid forcing expensive kernels into tight scheduling windows.
- Provide gradual rollout with observability and automatic rollback.

Proposed design (high level):
1) Jitter-aware admission limiter: maintain a short ring buffer of recent admission timestamps and compute a jitter metric (exponential-weighted percentile of inter-arrival variance). Admission threshold is adjusted dynamically by multiplying the token budget by a jitter-smoothing factor. During high jitter the limiter requires slightly larger batch formation windows for attention-heavy requests. This reduces the number of tiny, expensive kernels interleaved with large batches.

2) Attention micro-slicing: for models where attention compute dominates, enable an optional micro-slicing mode. Long decodes will expose attention work in micro-slices separated by short gaps (decode pulses). The runtime exposes hooks so the admission controller can schedule small short requests into those micro gaps without forcing kernel reinitialization. Micro-slicing is implemented as a cooperative yield at attention boundary kernels and uses existing KV cache interfaces.

3) Decode pacing and kernel-affinity hints: requests carry (or are inferred) a kernel-affinity hint (e.g., fp16-fused-attn, q4-quantized-attn). Admission prefers to co-locate requests that share kernel affinity within the same batch window. Decode pacing enforces a soft per-GPU token ingress rate to avoid sudden kernel switching; when kernel affinity conflicts are unavoidable we fallback to conservative scheduling (slower admission but stable latency).

4) Backpressure & fallbacks: implement a hop-by-hop backpressure signal from the batcher to API gateway to smooth client rate spikes (token-shed and retry-after semantics). Automatic fallback policy: if admission limiter detects sustained jitter beyond a threshold, degrade to a conservative kernel profile pool and route latency-sensitive requests to low-latency variants.

Measuring success:
- Primary metrics: p95/p99/request-tail (95th/99th/99.9th latency for token decode and end-to-end), tail-impact fraction (percentage of requests contributing to top 1% latency), and change in GPU utilization.
- Acceptance criteria for rollout: 25% reduction in p99 for mixed chat+long streaming workloads with <=3% regression in median latency and <=5% throughput loss on canary.

Implementation plan:
- Phase 1 (3 weeks): implement jitter metric, admission multiplier, and kernel-affinity hint plumbing. Unit tests + local microbench harness.
- Phase 2 (2 weeks): implement micro-slicing runtime hook and KV cache-safe yield points; integrate with admission limiter.
- Phase 3 (1 week): canary on dedicated pool with synthetic mixed workloads; collect metrics and iterate.
- Phase 4 (1 week): gradual rollout with feature flag, dashboarding, and default conservative thresholds.

Testing & validation:
- Synthetic mixes: chat-only (short tokens), long-stream-only (200–1000 tokens), and mixed (60/40 short/long).
- Kernel switch stress test: rapid alternation of affinity hints to validate backpressure behavior.
- Long-duration soak (48h) on a dedicated node to verify no throughput regression or memory leak.

Trade-offs and risks:
- Micro-slicing requires changes to attention kernels and coordination with KV cache; some models may not support safe yield points (risk: complexity and model incompatibility).
- Conservative admission increases latency for some requests; must tune smoothing factor carefully to avoid hurting p50.
- Kernel-affinity grouping can reduce fairness across tenants if not tenanted-aware; will add tenant quotas into heuristics if needed.

Rollout & observability:
- Dashboard: new Grafana panel "Jitter Admission" showing jitter metric, admission window, kernel-affinity mix, and p95/p99 by affinity.
- Canary gating: start in a single low-latency dedicated pool with feature flag 'jitter_admission_v1' and monitor thresholds for 24 hours. Auto rollback if regressions exceed thresholds.

Docs & artifacts:
- Design doc: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/INF/Jitter-Aware-Admission-and-Attention-Micro-Slicing
- PR stub: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/4218 (WIP)
- Benchmark dashboard: https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/latency/continuous-batching

Dependencies:
- Needs kernel refactor from ENG-17412 for attention yield points.
- Prefill shaping improvements in ENG-31247 will reduce pressure on admission limiter (low coupling).

Open questions:
- Which open models can safely expose micro-slicing (LLAMA variants vs GPT-style)? We should run a small model-compat matrix.
- Should tenant fairness be enforced at admission or at routing layer? Initial plan: admission with tenant-aware token budgets.
- How to expose kernel-affinity hints via public API without breaking backward compatibility? Suggest internal-only header for now and SDK opt-in later.
